main_point: The MPAA sued Usenet search sites without notifying them first, causing outrage among administrators who claim their sites are legal and would have cooperated had they been contacted properly.

statements.text: The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) has initiated legal action against seven specific website operators, asserting that these entities are facilitating the unauthorized distribution of copyrighted material. This public announcement marks the commencement of lawsuits against BitTorrent trackers and Usenet search engines, a move that bypasses direct notification to the site administrators.
statements.text_short: The MPAA publicly sued seven website operators for alleged copyright infringement without prior direct notification.

statements.text: The administrators of the Usenet search engine dvdrs.net state that they have not received any direct communication from the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) regarding the legal action taken against their site. They express deep outrage at this procedural failure, arguing that the public announcement of lawsuits without prior contact is an unacceptable method of enforcement that damages their reputation and trust.
statements.text_short: The dvdrs.net administrators claim they were not directly notified by the MPAA before public lawsuits were filed, causing them significant outrage.

statements.text: The administrators of the affected websites express shock and outrage that the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) chose to announce its lawsuits publicly rather than contacting them directly first. They assert that, had they been given proper prior notice, they would have cooperated fully with the MPAA's concerns and worked toward a resolution, indicating that the lack of direct communication is the primary issue.
statements.text_short: Website administrators express shock and outrage that the MPAA announced lawsuits publicly instead of contacting them directly, noting they would have cooperated with proper notice.

statements.text: The administrators of the Usenet search engine dvdrs.net emphasize that they would have willingly cooperated with the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) had the organization contacted them personally to discuss their concerns. However, they argue that being publicly portrayed as an established piracy ring without prior direct engagement is an outrage, as they maintain their site operates within international laws and has worked hard to comply with legal standards.
statements.text_short: The dvdrs.net administrators state they would have cooperated with the MPAA if contacted personally, but condemn the public portrayal of their site as a piracy ring.

statements.text: Although the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act provides a legal framework for addressing alleged copyright infringement, the administrators of the Binnews and dvdrs.net search sites claim they have established internal procedures to comply with such laws. However, these operators assert that they have never received any formal takedown notices from the copyright holders, despite the existence of these legal mechanisms.
statements.text_short: Usenet site administrators claim they have legal procedures to handle infringement but deny receiving any takedown notices.

statements.text: The administrators of the Binnews search site explicitly state that they have never received a copyright infringement notice from any organization, despite maintaining proper guidelines for handling Digital Millennium Copyright Act requests on their platform.
statements.text_short: Binnews administrators confirm they have never received any copyright infringement notices from any organization.

statements.text: The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) initiated lawsuits against Usenet search sites without first notifying the site administrators, a procedural failure that has caused significant outrage among the operators. These administrators argue that their sites operate legally and would have cooperated fully with the MPAA to resolve the issues had they been contacted directly and properly before the public announcement.
statements.text_short: The MPAA sued Usenet sites without prior notice, causing outrage among administrators who claim their sites are legal and would have cooperated had they been contacted properly.

statements.text: The operators of the dvdrs.net search site assert that they would immediately delete any offending files upon receiving a formal request and would conduct a thorough investigation into any connected files. They emphasize that they are fully committed to complying with legal standards and would respond personally to any valid takedown notices to resolve the matter efficiently.
statements.text_short: The dvdrs.net operators assert they would immediately delete offending files and conduct thorough research upon receiving a formal request.

statements.text: Administrators of Usenet search sites like Binnews and Dvdrs assert that their platforms operate legally by indexing files already hosted on commercial, tax-paying companies rather than storing the content themselves, functioning similarly to standard search engines. They maintain that without the premium services of these third-party hosts, their text-based indexes would be useless, arguing that they merely point to existing files without hosting illegal material directly.
statements.text_short: Usenet site administrators assert their platforms operate legally by indexing files from commercial hosts rather than storing content directly.

statements.text: The Descds administration contends that if the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) considers their Usenet indexing service unlawful, they must also sue premium paid Usenet providers that function as file carriers. This position points out a perceived inconsistency, observing that large providers such as Easynews and Usenetserver provide both indexing and carrier services but have not faced lawsuits from the MPAA.
statements.text_short: The Descds administration maintains that if the MPAA decides their service is unlawful, they must also go after premium paid Usenet providers, since those providers handle the transfer of these files.

statements.text: The Descds administration expresses frustration that Newzbin, the creators and promoters of the NZB format and arguably the largest Usenet indexing site in the world, has not been sued by the MPAA. They describe their situation as being 'rail roaded' and unhappy about the selective legal approach, contrasting their treatment with the lack of action against the primary source of the indexing format.
statements.text_short: The Descds administration expresses frustration that Newzbin, the largest Usenet indexing site, has not been sued by the MPAA, describing their situation as being unfairly targeted.

statements.text: Although the Descds administration operates outside of US jurisdiction, they state they are willing to assist the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) in resolving the legal dispute. They offer to remove any sections deemed illegal immediately upon receiving communication and legal judgment, while simultaneously hoping the MPAA will retract its claim that they are an organized pirate network and restore their reputation.
statements.text_short: Although operating outside US jurisdiction, the Descds administration states they are willing to assist the MPAA in resolving the legal dispute by removing illegal content upon request.

statements.text: The entity operating the Dvdrs.net website asserts that its service does not constitute a pirate network, despite the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) labeling it as such. This claim relies on the premise that the site merely indexes files hosted by others rather than distributing them directly, arguing that the accusation misrepresents the organization's actual function and damages its reputation as a legitimate community resource.
statements.text_short: Dvdrs.net denies being a pirate network, arguing its indexing service is legitimate and the MPAA's accusation is false.

statements.text: Although the Dvdrs.net server is physically located in the United States, the operator emphasizes that they are a British citizen and therefore not legally bound by US communications regulations or judicial judgments. This distinction is used to argue that the US-based Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) lacks the legal authority to enforce its claims against the operator, suggesting that the organization's resolve to comply depends entirely on establishing proper communication and jurisdictional respect.
statements.text_short: The Dvdrs.net operator argues that their UK citizenship exempts them from US laws, challenging the MPAA's legal authority to enforce its claims.

statements.text: The administrators of the Dvdrs.net website state that they would be willing to remove specific files if the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) had approached them directly and professionally before initiating legal action. They contend that the lack of prior notification and the immediate lawsuit created an unnecessary conflict, asserting that a proper dialogue would have allowed the site to cooperate and resolve the issue without litigation.
statements.text_short: Dvdrs.net administrators claim they would have cooperated with the MPAA if they had been contacted properly before the lawsuit.

statements.text: The leadership behind the Dvdrs.net website expresses a strong desire for the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) to retract its public statement labeling the site as an organized pirate network. They argue that this accusation is factually incorrect and has caused significant harm to the site's reputation and the trust of its member base, urging the industry group to restore the organization's good name through a retraction.
statements.text_short: Dvdrs.net leadership urges the MPAA to retract its false accusation and restore the site's reputation.

statements.text: The operators of Binnews assert that the service does not host any copyrighted files, explicitly rejecting the accusation that the site distributes over 3,000 movies as entirely false. They maintain that their platform provides a legitimate utility to copyright holders rather than facilitating infringement, arguing that the site's actual function is to assist rights owners in managing their intellectual property. This denial serves as a direct rebuttal to the premise that the site is an illegal repository of pirated content.
statements.text_short: Binnews operators deny hosting files and claim their service legitimately assists copyright holders.

statements.text: The administrators of Binnews insist that their primary intent has never been to facilitate piracy, arguing instead that they offer specific guides designed to help companies eliminate it. They contend that their service acts as a tool for rights holders to track and remove infringing content from Usenet networks, positioning the platform as a proactive solution to copyright infringement rather than a source of illegal downloads. This stance frames the conflict as a misunderstanding of the site's actual purpose and value to the entertainment industry.
statements.text_short: Binnews administrators claim their intent is to help companies stop piracy, not facilitate it.

statements.text: The creators of Dvdrs.net explain that the website originated in March 2004 as a general community forum for discussing movies and home cinema issues, evolving into a Usenet indexing service only after user requests. They emphasize that the site was never contacted by legal representatives prior to the lawsuit, arguing that the absence of prior notification suggests the legal action is premature and ignores the site's initial legitimate community roots. This narrative frames the dispute as a failure of proper communication rather than evidence of inherent illegal activity.
statements.text_short: Dvdrs.net administrators describe the site's origins as a legitimate community forum and note a lack of prior legal contact.
